title: Choosing a CMS when the marketing team is small
metaTitle: A CMS for a small marketing team
excerpt: A CMS for a small marketing team should match who edits, how often, and whether drafts matter. A tool the founder will not open is not a publishing system.
primaryKeyword: cms for a small marketing team
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window. The hands on the keys fit a piece about the person who will actually edit the site.
caption: Choose the tool for the person who edits, not for the feature list. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a small team choose a CMS?
faqs.answer: Name who will edit, how often they will edit, and whether a draft needs review before it is public. If one founder changes a headline a few times a year, files in the repository may be enough. If someone publishes every week, they need an editor, a preview, and a draft. Buy the tool that matches that rhythm.

faqs.question: Do we need a CMS on day one?
faqs.answer: Not always. A fixed marketing site can store its pages in the codebase and still be easy for a developer to update. Add a CMS when a non-developer must publish, or when drafts and schedules become the work. Adding one on day one because every site has one creates a system nobody logs into.

faqs.question: What should the CMS not be allowed to do?
faqs.answer: It should not let every page become a free-form canvas. Structured fields for the headline, the sections, and the images keep the design intact. Absolute freedom on layout is how a small team slowly dismantles the site it just paid for.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A CMS for a small marketing team is a fit question, not a feature contest. Decide who edits, how often they edit, and whether a draft must exist before something is public. The tool that matches those three will get used. The tool with the longer brochure will sit behind a login nobody remembers.

A small team is often one founder and, on a good week, one other person who can write. They do not have an editorial operations group. They have a site that must stay true, and a limited patience for software that feels like a second product.

## Who edits

If the only editor is a developer, a CMS may be a layer you do not need yet. Pages can live in the repository, reviewed like any other change, and deployed when they are ready. The cost is that a non-developer cannot safely publish on a Saturday. If that cost is acceptable, pay it. You will have fewer systems to maintain.

If the editor is a founder or a marketer who should not need a pull request, the CMS is the product they touch. Sit them in it before you buy it. Have them change a real headline, replace a real image, and find the page again the next day. A demo with sample content hides the friction. Their own sentence reveals it.

Write down the editor's name. A CMS chosen for a hypothetical future hire will be shaped for a person who is not here, and the person who is here will work around it. You can change tools later, when that hire exists. You cannot get back the month spent configuring a newsroom workflow for a company of three.

## How often

Frequency decides the weight of the tool. A site that changes a few times a year can afford a slightly clumsy path, even a developer path, because the clumsiness is rare. A blog, a changelog, or a set of landing pages that must move every week cannot. The weekly editor will abandon a clumsy tool, or they will paste everything into one rich-text box and destroy the layout.

Match the fields to the frequency. The things that change often get obvious fields: title, summary, body, image, date. The things that change rarely, such as the navigation or the footer, can stay in code, where a rare change gets a review. Putting the entire site into the CMS, including the parts nobody should improvise, is how a small team gains freedom it will misuse under deadline.

Hanabi's own writing sits in Payload, separate from the client portal. The articles have drafts. The portal holds brand files, docs, and project updates for clients. Those are different jobs, done by different people, and they do not share a login. A company site deserves the same honesty. Public pages in the publishing tool. Private delivery somewhere else. One login for everything feels simple until the wrong person can edit the wrong thing.

## Whether drafts matter

Drafts matter when more than one person must see a page before it is public, or when the writer is also the person who would be embarrassed by a typo on the homepage. A draft and a preview are the whole workflow many small teams need. A calendar of states, approvals, and roles is a different product.

If you publish straight from the editor with no preview, you will publish mistakes, because the editing view is never the page. Require a preview on the real template. The headline wrapping, the image crop, and the title element are visible there or they are visible to the customer. Prefer the first.

Google's notes on [title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) are a concrete requirement for the CMS, not a search trivia card. Every page needs a title element. The text should be descriptive and distinct, not a vague label and not the same boilerplate on every URL. If your editor cannot set a title per page, and see it in the preview, you will ship a site Google has to retitle from whatever text it can find. That field belongs in the draft, next to the headline, because the headline and the title are related and not always identical.

## A small set of options

Choose among a few shapes, and refuse the middle muddle.

- Pages in the repository, edited by a developer, for a site that rarely changes.
- A CMS with structured fields and drafts, for a person who publishes often and should not touch layout.
- A page builder, only if you accept that layout will drift and you are willing to police it. Most small teams are not.

Hanabi's public site is built in Next.js. The blog is the part that needs an editor and a draft. The marketing pages are more stable. That split is a legitimate answer. Your split might be different. The mistake is one tool forced to do every job, including jobs you do not have.

Ask who hosts the CMS and who owns the content if you leave. A tool you do not control, holding the only copy of your pages, is a dependency. Export, or a repository that still contains the content, should be part of the choice. A founder should be able to take the words with them.

## What to ignore in the comparison chart

Ignore the count of integrations. You need the form destination you actually use, not a directory of a hundred. Ignore themes. A theme is a design you will throw away, and it says nothing about the editor. Ignore a promise that non-technical people can build anything. They can, and the site will show it. You wanted them to edit the things that change, inside a design that stays.

Ignore a requirement to pick the tool the developer's last client used, unless it also fits your editor and your frequency. Familiarity is a real advantage for the person building. It is not an advantage if the founder will not log in.

The trade between a custom page and a builder is the decision hiding under a lot of CMS sales. [How to keep a site editable without a page-builder mess](/blog/editable-without-a-page-builder) is the next piece. It argues for fields on the things that change, and for keeping the pixels in the design.

When you want the site and the editing path chosen together, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). A small team needs a publisher it will actually open, not a system that looks complete in a diagram.
